title.en: Weighted mean and stacked bar charts

text.en: In a school, the final exam counts for more than a quiz. To combine such scores fairly we give each its weight.

The weighted mean of x1, x2, ..., xn with weights w1, w2, ..., wn is (w1 x1 + w2 x2 + ... + wn xn) divided by (w1 + w2 + ... + wn).
Use it whenever parts of the data have different numbers of values or different importance, such as combining marks of assessments.
An average of averages can be found with weights equal to the number of values in each group.
The weighted mean also gives the mean when some values are added or removed, and the concentration of mixtures.
A stacked bar chart puts parts on top of one another, useful when the total of each bar also matters.
A 100% stacked bar chart compares proportions, like a pie chart, not absolute values.
From a stacked bar chart you can make a 100% stacked chart, but not the other way round.
Always check the weights add to the right total.

problem.en: A quiz (weight 1) score is 60 and an exam (weight 3) score is 80. Find the weighted mean.

why.en: Multiply each score by its weight.

prompt.en: When do we use a weighted mean?

requiredIdeas.en: Multiply by weights then divide by total weight

commonMisconceptions.en: Using the simple mean when weights differ

points.en: Weighted mean = sum of (weight x value) / sum of weights.
It handles unequal importance or group sizes.
Stacked bars show totals; 100% stacked bars show proportions.
A 100% chart cannot be turned back into a stacked chart.
